section.title: David Fowler: Microsoft Promotions, Permissionless Projects, and the Distinguished Engineer Path
section.deck: Microsoft distinguished engineer David Fowler explains how building prototypes without permission, learning to delegate, and focusing on impact over cleverness carried him from intern to distinguished engineer.

blocks.text: David Fowler, a Microsoft distinguished engineer, tells the host that his climb from intern to distinguished engineer came from building working prototypes without waiting for permission, then learning to scale through other people instead of through his own typing. In Fowler's account, impact matters more than cleverness at every level, mentors who are blunt about how promotion decisions get made are worth seeking out, and several habits that carry an engineer to senior can block the move beyond it. The talk also covers debugging, the culture change after Satya Nadella became CEO, and why Fowler stayed at one company. Everything below is Fowler's account of his own experience unless marked as an editorial note.
blocks.heading: Fowler's view: build things, scale through others, and let impact drive promotion

blocks.question: How does Microsoft's leveling system work, given that levels run upward from 59 with about two levels per title?
answer: Fowler says he cannot explain why numbering starts at 59, and guesses the lower levels cover non-engineering roles. A college graduate typically starts at 59 or 60, depending on how many times they interned and how well they did. Fowler equates entry level with an SDE I at other companies.

A title maps to a band of about two levels, so a title does not reveal which level someone holds. Principal is the exception at three levels, and Fowler says that band is so broad that a new arrival from senior and a long-serving principal share a title. Above principal come the partner levels, which Fowler says have three bands, and then technical fellow.
blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: How did you end up at Microsoft?
answer: Fowler grew up in Barbados and left at 18 for Florida Tech, chosen partly because it held career fairs and was one flight from home. He started in computer engineering, decided after the first class that it was not for him because he wanted to code, and switched to computer science. He had been coding since about age ten, and was surprised that no one in the first Java class knew how to code.

Fowler and a close friend built games on nights and weekends. To stand out at their first career fair, they brought a laptop with a game demo. That produced about four internship offers. Fowler chose Microsoft over GE and smaller Florida firms, and the friend went to EA. After campus interviews and an in-person whiteboard round, he interned in 2006 and 2007, which he found eye-opening.

followups.question: What was it like going to Bill Gates's house as an intern?
answer: Fowler says every intern group traditionally ended the summer there, and he was in the last set to go. Interns had phones taken and were bused in from a church parking area. He was chatting when a rush of interns ran toward him, and Gates was standing behind him. Fowler shook Gates's hand and says they spoke once.
followups.speaker: David Fowler

followups.question: What did the Microsoft interview process look like in 2006?
answer: Fowler says Microsoft was known for puzzle questions, citing the book How Would You Move Mount Fuji? and the manhole-cover question. His interview began with an easy coding question on paper, then a puzzle about making exactly four gallons from a three-gallon and a five-gallon jug. He had seen the film scene but could not recall the steps, and worked them out. The last question was how to count the gas stations in Florida. He asked whether it was a trick question, was told no, and saw no point. He thought it had gone badly but got a call back.

The host adds that LeetCode-style questions at least relate to the job, and recalls being asked to add two numbers in base negative two. Both agree interviewing has changed a lot, in some ways for the better and in some for the worse.
followups.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: What is the story behind NuGet, the .NET package manager?
answer: Fowler says NuGet is now more than ten years old, and its impact today feels jarring compared with its start. The team was building a new web stack to compete with the LAMP stack, and Fowler did not question whether that made sense, because the leaders above him said to do it. Ruby on Rails and its gems had just arrived, and another group was looking at WordPress and Drupal, which also had packages. The consensus was that the platform needed a package manager so people could extend it.

The first version was an in-browser package manager in the style of WordPress. In a meeting with Scott Guthrie, whom Fowler describes as an EVP now, a product manager showed a PowerPoint mockup. Fowler and an architect had already built something and asked whether the team could start from there. That meeting formed the NuGet team: Fowler as first engineer, the architect David Ebbo, and Phil Haack. They also talked with people behind other open-source .NET package managers.
blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: What did your performance review look like after NuGet, for someone who was not yet a senior engineer?
answer: Fowler's first promotion came about eight months after joining, before NuGet. Because he had interned twice, he arrived with a lot of Microsoft experience. Beyond assigned work, he read forums for feedback on Microsoft's products, built features to answer it, and showed the results to product managers, architects and the team. Looking back, he says those people became sponsors and positioned him to build NuGet.

Fowler calls himself a code-first, ask-questions-later person and says code is currency: a working sample beats a PowerPoint or a document. A director once told him he would send people to talk to David because David has energy.

followups.question: Did the lasting impact of something like NuGet carry over into later reviews?
answer: Fowler says the bigger promotions felt like accumulated history plus current success. Impact is officially meant to be for the year, and crossing a band boundary, such as to senior or to principal, takes more than moving within a band. He is unsure whether Microsoft has an official deferred-impact rule, but says it clearly mattered at the higher principal levels, where the question was whether he had shown repeated impact over ten years.
followups.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: How did SignalR start?
answer: Fowler says the name came from the era when web products dropped letters from their names. The project began on nights and weekends. Google Docs had just appeared, and Fowler was enthralled by smooth co-editing. He set out to build Google Docs for code, did not finish it, but learned about WebSockets, which he says had not shipped yet, and how to build that kind of app.

Damian Edwards, a product manager, was building a talk on long-running streaming apps in .NET. Fowler proposed building a library together. Microsoft allows moonlighting on projects outside official work, so the two worked until midnight and open-sourced it, and people started using it. Later a product manager said it should be made official.

Fowler calls it the first thing built from his own idea, after years of working on other people's ideas. He became a pseudo tech lead without ever being a manager, hired college graduates, and at one point led a team of about eight.

followups.question: What pushed you to give up weekends and late nights for it?
answer: Fowler had not seen anything like it. Google Docs was the first product of its kind to work that well, and Node.js with Socket.IO showed a new way to push data from server to client. The project hit limits deep in the core platform and taught him a lot about the networking stack. He says the volume of problems was like catnip.
followups.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: How can others start projects like this within a large company, when the motivation comes entirely from them?
answer: Fowler's one-sentence answer is that you can just do things, which people now call agency. He does not recommend spending every night and weekend on projects, but early on his goal was to get better at software engineering, and the way was to build everything possible: games, websites, many kinds of software.

The second habit was to find someone on the team whose career he wanted. Fowler attached himself to the architect David Ebbo, whose role spanned several areas and looked ahead, copied his behaviors, and for a while coded Ebbo's ideas, which turned into doing it independently. He then built prototypes and showed them to an advocate, the architect or the product manager, to ask whether they were useful. He says he would build a thousand things and maybe one would hit.

followups.question: So agency at a big company came from energy, moonlighting and doing more than the assigned work?
answer: Fowler agrees in part. Once an engineer builds a reputation for building things, more opportunities arrive and people ask for a take on new work. He cautions that this is not guaranteed, but in his case it was clearly true and continued after SignalR.
followups.speaker: David Fowler

followups.question: Is permissionless agency a way to bypass the credibility that permissioned opportunities require?
answer: The host puts it that way, and the exchange adds that a stronger track record earns more room to be permissionless, because each success buys more latitude to fail. The host describes fast-growing engineers as trusted people management lets loose on risky projects, while an engineer struggling to meet expectations gets directed work and monitoring. Fowler agrees.
followups.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: What led to the promotion to principal?
answer: Fowler recalls a boss who, when he reached senior, said promotions would slow. The jump to principal turned out to be large. Alongside SignalR, he built Kudu, an early Azure tool that let people push code and deploy an app instantly, as Heroku and AppHarbor did. A director then pulled him onto a new project that became the cross-platform .NET Core.

Fowler was senior, and he and another principal engineer were chosen as architects over about 30 engineers with free rein, which he calls amazing and terrifying. At first he tried to code review every change and was burnt out within a year, and had to learn to trust people and separate urgent from not urgent. He had his first child and was promoted to principal that same year.

followups.question: How did you scale yourself out of necessity so you did not burn out as architect for so many engineers?
answer: Fowler learned the first lessons on SignalR, a team of seven or eight including two new hires. Before that he never delegated to grow someone and assumed he could do the work faster himself. It flipped when he saw that investing in smart new hires would amplify impact even if early tasks took longer. He calls the senior-to-principal leap doing more through others than yourself, and the point where many engineers plateau because they prefer coding alone.

On .NET Core, where he says the team rebuilt the package manager, runtime and libraries from scratch, he stopped treating everything as equally urgent and let people fail. He says traits that get an engineer to senior, such as being a control freak or insisting on one way, hurt when scaling to a thousand engineers. The fix was to inspire others through one-on-ones and example, and to become outcome-focused.
followups.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: What does the architect role mean at Microsoft?
answer: Fowler says it is a semi-official role open to the middle principal bands. When he joined, he saw a principal software architect and decided that was the role he wanted. He describes it as breadth over depth: overseeing the design of the whole system. Other archetypes at the top include a super coder who builds enormous amounts, deep specialists such as one of the leading garbage-collection experts working on the .NET collector, and people overseeing a hugely impactful product area.

As architect for ASP.NET Core, he oversaw the web framework, the web server and how packages shipped, vetting decisions that could last 20 years. He had not done this before and learned by shadowing mentors who had.
blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: As a distinguished engineer, how has the share of your time spent writing code changed?
answer: Fowler says the job may no longer reward daily coding, but selfishly he codes every day and currently sends many pull requests on a project involving Aspire. He does not want to be an architect who gives instructions without knowing the code and then disappears. He wants to be a peer on the team, facing the builds and the tests.

followups.question: If you stopped coding and only led, would your performance review still look fine?
answer: Fowler thinks so. A distinguished engineer is measured on organization-wide or company-wide impact, so part of the job is keeping the architecture sound, looking ahead, talking publicly, inspiring and mentoring. He gave four internal talks on using AI for software engineering, which began when someone asked after seeing him use it. He argues such talks matter because credible engineers explaining how they work persuade more than a boss giving orders.
followups.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: What is the story behind the promotion to distinguished engineer?
answer: Fowler calls it the craziest promotion he has experienced. Distinguished engineer is the last level within partner, and it comes through an official process, not an annual review: a set of technical leaders peer-reviews the candidate. Guido van Rossum, who created Python, is at the same level, and Fowler describes maximum imposter syndrome. He also thought he was young for the role, though that did not count against him.

Fowler says earlier work carried it, because the role requires a body of work and a track record, not one good year. The email promoting him from principal to partner cited .NET Core, by then about seven years old, and he had acted as architect helping many teams adopt the new .NET internally. NuGet and SignalR counted as signals of how what he helped build affected the industry and the company. He says the fellows decide.

followups.question: Were you involved in that process, or was it a surprise?
answer: Fowler helped his leadership with content, supplying papers he had written and code contributions, and did nothing else. What affected him most was hearing other fellows say the promotion was well deserved and about time.
followups.speaker: David Fowler

followups.question: Do you worry about the lofty expectations of the level now that you have held it for a while?
answer: At first Fowler called himself a baby DE. After roughly two and a half to three years he feels confident he can perform at the level. In his first review cycle he felt pressure to document all impact and tell his boss, because the level sits just below executive. He found a pattern of talking to bosses and staying visible, and feels less pressure now, though he adds that things could change.
followups.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: What does the final level, technical fellow, look like?
answer: Fowler says people at that level are unicorns with different paths, so the useful move is to look for proxies for impact, not copy anyone. A fellow needs industry-wide impact. His examples: Anders Hejlsberg, whom people in his division idolize, made Turbo Pascal, Delphi, C# and TypeScript. Dave Cutler, who Fowler says built Windows NT, the Azure operating system and the Xbox hypervisor, is the only senior technical fellow, a title Fowler says is simply his own.

Fowler adds that Microsoft recently hired a fellow who invented RSS, and that a teammate was once an intern for Tim Berners-Lee and is on the HTTP specification. These are Fowler's own statements and were not checked against other sources.
blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: Were there unexpected perks of becoming a distinguished engineer?
answer: Fowler says the best perk is an email alias called engineer that reaches every distinguished engineer at Microsoft. There is also an internal forum where they meet every couple of months. Access typically works through a sponsor, and when he became a partner he asked management for a mentor who was a fellow, reasoning that anyone wanting to become one should have fellows as mentors.

One was Jeffrey Snover, who invented PowerShell and, Fowler says, recently left Microsoft for Google. Fowler calls him one of his best mentors and a main sponsor, and he attended one of the technical leaders' forums as a result.
blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: What did that mentor say that made a difference?
answer: Fowler says much career advice is vague, such as telling someone to do a super impactful project, whereas Snover was direct. He suggested going to the people who decide, including the CTOs, and asking what the role requires. Fowler found it jarring, since no one had told him to ask the source, but very helpful, because it showed him what he should and should not be doing.

A second mentor helped after Fowler received a feedback package from his manager and peers listing strengths, weaknesses and behavior under stress. His first reaction was to fix every weakness. The mentor said to amplify his strengths instead, because no one is promoted to these roles for being average. About five years ago this changed how Fowler works. He now builds teams around his gaps: he does not schedule meetings or run every shipping checklist, and makes sure someone who is good at that does. The host likens this to a power law, and Fowler agrees.
blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: Which engineers do you look up to, and what makes them impressive?
answer: Fowler's team includes about five other partner-level engineers with more than 20 years at the company, each excellent for a different reason: a garbage-collector expert, a super coder who he says is a true 10x engineer, someone who seems to know obscure details across C, compilers and the operating system, and others with a strong eye for what to build.

On the C# language design review team, Fowler sits with Hejlsberg, whose feedback he says never talks down and stays pragmatic, even though the code Hejlsberg commits looks like it is inventing theory no one has seen. Fowler also names Mark Russinovich, CTO of Azure, who still codes and recently emailed about a performance improvement he wrote. Fowler is inspired when senior engineers still code.

He warns about the meeting trap. After becoming partner, he sat in meetings all day and was sad. A mentor told him an individual contributor needs time to think and build, and to block at least eight hours a week. It took him a while to learn to decline meetings.
blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: If you designed a university course on refactoring, what would its key concepts be?
answer: Fowler says computer science is not software engineering. A first job involves a lot of time understanding what exists so the first change can be surgical and not break the build. He would put students in an artificially large codebase, changed every year so they cannot copy earlier work, and ask them to fix a bug and write a test. Working out where to put code, he argues, builds skills a LeetCode question or textbook exercise does not.

Each assignment could be a single fix. Fowler notes that many jobs are about tweaking existing software, and even someone working on Windows is unlikely to change the kernel unless building a new operating system.
blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: Why do you say the high-leverage skill is debugging rather than writing new code, even though interviews focus on writing?
answer: Early on, Fowler worked with platform engineers on the .NET team and watched them diagnose crashes, race conditions and threading issues. He concluded that shipping an app and handling crash reports and production problems calls for a second skill set, distinct from authoring code. He would like an interview that hands a candidate a crash dump, to see what they start doing, such as adding logs, rerunning, reasoning about race conditions or printing thread ids, not whether they solve it.

He tells of an early-Azure night at 1 a.m. when his CVP messaged asking if he was free, and he was added to a call of about a hundred engineers trying to work out why a very popular site was crashing. It turned out to be a concurrency problem in a dictionary. Fowler concludes that writing code is a small piece of an engineer's skill set.

followups.question: What about the fixer archetype, who makes a one-line change after heavy investigation?
answer: The host describes the fixer as someone who drops in and makes a one-line change that makes something two or three times better. Fowler says someone on his team does this: when a thread starts about a performance issue in a gRPC call, he adds that engineer, who returns a trace and solves it.
followups.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: What prompted your lukewarm take that the lower you sit on the technology stack, the fewer mistakes you are allowed to make?
answer: Fowler works on the platform, and says changes there break services in ways that people higher up would find unheard of. Changing the order in which a method returns results, for example, can take down a company's website. He suspects the tweet followed a bug found during first-party adoption of .NET, where upgrading teams hit issues that shocked him, such as a method with about 400 arguments reaching a limit.
blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: You tweeted that when promoted to senior you felt others were smarter and should have gone first. What did you take from that?
answer: Fowler worried about being promoted early on a fast path. His team had four people from MIT and two from Carnegie Mellon, and he had gone to Florida Tech, so he worked through imposter syndrome by working very hard.

The promotion taught him that impact is not about being the smartest, but about whether the work is at the top of the business, as NuGet and SignalR were. He had always felt he needed to go deeper on some technology, and now asks whether that is for you or for your career. He says an engineer does not need to know how TCP/IP works to be promoted to senior. It helped him separate being smart from making impact.
Co-workers were happy for him, at least outwardly. When he asked about others who had risen fast, he was told everyone knew it would happen, and he adds that you never know which category you are in.
blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: One of your big-company tips is to ask when the last reorg was before changing roles. What is the thinking behind that?
answer: Fowler calls big companies machines and recalls hearing, perhaps tongue in cheek, that executives show motion through reorgs. A reorg is always coming or has just happened, so learn about the last one: who the leaders are, what triggered it and where the org is heading. Because Microsoft is so big, he says, every new org is effectively a new company. The tweet likely followed a mentee who had been reorged several times in a row, or something that happened to him.

followups.question: Is this about reading what a reorg means for your future?
answer: Yes. Fowler also relays advice he heard recently: when changing jobs, think about what you hate, not what you love, because the things you love will be easy. Someone who hates open offices should not join a company with open-plan seating.
followups.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: What has kept you at Microsoft for so long, since your internships?
answer: Fowler describes himself as part of a millennial generation that broke from the boomer-parent habit of staying in one place forever, and says many job-hopping friends were paid well for it. His closest call came when he was senior and a boss who had left for pre-IPO Twitter asked him to interview there. He interviewed at Twitter and GitHub, got both offers, and stayed after much deliberation. The morning Twitter went public, he adds, brought instant depression that lasted about a week.

Microsoft's counteroffer was fine but not the main reason. An executive vice president told him he would be a distinguished engineer in five years, which Fowler says oversold it. What mattered more was that he had built something impactful and permissionless and had gained autonomy, and leaving meant starting over. People overlook the network and track record they have built, and the people matter as much as pay: not just good engineers but good people to work with.
He also stayed because he got to work on something new about every two years, by design, which kept him from feeling the need to go elsewhere.

followups.question: If a mentee at Microsoft had a pre-IPO offer from a company like OpenAI, would you say stay or go?
answer: Fowler would tell them to go. He recalls a mentee with an offer from another company who was not in a place to do their best work, and told that mentee to leave despite any counteroffer. He says that, in the same situation himself, he might have gone.
followups.speaker: David Fowler

followups.question: You tweeted that once in a career you should stay on a project long enough to see the long-term impact of your decisions. What prompted that?
answer: Fowler's career had been to work on something and move on, still helping those who took over. .NET Core, at about ten years, is the longest he has worked on anything. Seeing the effects of decisions made in the first two years, good or bad, gave him a new perspective. He jokes that on a ten-year project every small issue you postponed becomes a big one, because somebody will hit all of it.

He is unsure twenty years on one project is good for career growth, but says it teaches you the implications of your choices and what you would fix in the next version. The host wonders what a chain of ever-higher jumps does for judgment if each project declines after the person leaves. Fowler does not fault either path and has done both. He cannot name the ingredients of a successful project, but can tell when he is on one, like a fine-tuned internal model built over experience.
followups.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: Did you notice the culture shifting internally when Satya Nadella became CEO?
answer: Fowler says the shift was huge, but it is hard to see the jump from Steve Ballmer's era because he lived through it and it happened gradually. A big one was that, historically, two teams could work toward the same end state and one would win. Under Nadella the focus moved to collaboration over being first. He saw teams building solutions before knowing the problem, though not on his own team.

He describes changes in meetings, email and remote friendliness. He remembers being surprised by someone raising a hand in a Teams meeting, having grown up in a culture where you wait for a pause and talk. Earlier meetings were often a highest-paid-person's-opinion affair, where a loud senior person could stop others from feeling safe to speak. Early in his career he saw people shouting and wondered whether he would have to shout too. Now leaders model behavior such as inviting quiet people to share their views.

Collaboration also became part of reviews: engineers who avoided other teams' work, or cloned it, were marked down. The host summarizes this as a change driven by performance incentives and top-down messaging, and Fowler adds the behaviors leaders modeled. The host recalls the XKCD comic that draws Microsoft as people pointing guns at each other. Fowler says the real shift went from guns to ambivalence, with teams staying out of each other's way, and then to rewarded collaboration.
blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: Looking back, do you have major regrets people can learn from?
answer: Fowler says no major ones, but early in his career he was very arrogant and lacked empathy, and the tone of old GitHub comments would show it. Building teams and influencing through others taught him patience and empathy. Being right is only one of many things, he says, and software engineering has many shades of gray. He has more self-awareness now, though it still creeps out occasionally.

He names as a possible regret that he did not take early opportunities at Twitter or Facebook, which would have paid a lot for a senior engineer. A smaller regret outside the career: a friend messaged him in 2008 about starting a Bitcoin company, and he dismissed the idea. The host jokes that the friend must now hold a lot of Bitcoin.
blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: What was your work-life balance like throughout your career?
answer: Fowler used to say there was no balance, just working hard and playing hard. A comment he found useful recently is that balance is not about stopping at five o'clock but about what gives you energy and what drains it. He works a lot because programming is a passion as well as a job, and dials back now and then. Once he came back from vacation and began making games for fun, then took what he learned into work.

What drains him is meetings that feel purposeless. If he were in meetings all day and then went home to do the work he wanted to do, that would feel like burnout. He sees being paid to code as a privilege and plans to keep doing it until he can no longer.

followups.question: Is intrinsic motivation the unfair advantage behind careers like yours?
answer: The host says almost every very successful engineer seems to have it. Fowler agrees and recalls a talk by Andrej Karpathy about how much practice it takes to get good at anything (the captions garble the figure Fowler cited, so it is not reproduced here). Asked which book made him good, Fowler says he wrote and read a lot of code, and is not sure that is good advice but did not get good from a blog post.

His advice is to build everything: databases, distributed systems, games. He calls his GitHub a graveyard of projects, each of which taught a skill that only showed later. At 16 he tried to build a Street Fighter clone with art found online, purely to learn how a fighting game and key combos work. That need to understand how things work has lasted to this day.
followups.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.speaker: David Fowler

blocks.question: If you could advise yourself when graduating college and entering the industry, what would you say?
answer: Fowler's answer is to negotiate the salary. He did not know it was possible when he took his first job. A new graduate should get multiple offers and push the number up. Coming from Barbados and grateful for the most money he had seen, he was shocked to watch friends decline offers and say they would check Google or Facebook first. Having since sat on hiring committees for interns, he finds it impressive to watch a candidate bump up an offer well.
blocks.speaker: David Fowler
